1. The animation shows how a fixed income payment loses buying power as prices rise. It tests this against US history, using many possible starting months. The question is whether a payment that starts at a given level has "kept up" with inflation over time.

2. In frame 1, a single bar chart runs from 1947 to Aug 2006. It starts at a "first check" level and falls to a much lower level. This looks like purchasing power eroding after one starting month. Frames 2 and 3 show many starting months at once, 715 in total, for two inflation measures. CPI-U shows 17 of 715 kept up, and CPI-W (the index Social Security uses) shows 21 of 715. The few teal bars mark the starting months where payments kept up. Frames 4 to 6 add a third measure, PCE from 1959. It shows 19.2% kept up, against a "typical" 88.0%, and a larger teal block appears in the later years.

3. For most starting months in this history, a payment that stays fixed, or doesn't adjust enough, ended up buying less than the first check did. Only a small number of starting months kept up, mostly early ones. The PCE measure is the exception, since it shows a much larger share of kept-up months. The label "typical 88.0%" is not explained in the image, so I can't say what it compares against. The chart is marked "ILLUSTRATIVE" and "US only · history, not a forecast."

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer could reasonably take away that inflation can erode a fixed payout over time. That would make a payout with inflation adjustment worth a closer look, though it would likely start lower. The viewer would also see that the result depends on which inflation measure is used.

5. The animation did not suggest that advice. It only shows the data and the "history, not a forecast" caveat. The advice in 4 is my own conclusion.
